Random Cloud: Finding Minimal Neural Architectures Without Training

Javier Gil Blázquez Email: javgilbla@proton.me
Abstract

I propose the Random Cloud method, a training-free approach to neural architecture search that discovers minimal feedforward network topologies through stochastic exploration and progressive structural reduction. Unlike post-training pruning methods that require a full train-prune-retrain cycle, this method evaluates randomly initialized networks without backpropagation, progressively reduces their topology, and only trains the best minimal candidate at the end. I evaluate on 7 classification benchmarks against magnitude pruning and random pruning baselines. The Random Cloud matches or outperforms both baselines in 6 of 7 datasets, achieving statistically significant improvements on Sonar (+4.9+4.9pp accuracy, p=0.017p{=}0.017 vs magnitude pruning) with 87% parameter reduction. Crucially, the method is faster than both pruning baselines in 4 of 5 datasets (0.67–0.94×\times the cost of full training), since it avoids training the full-size network entirely.

1 Introduction

Finding the minimal neural network topology for a given task is a fundamental problem in machine learning. Overparameterized networks waste computation and memory, while underparameterized ones underfit. The standard approach is to start large and prune: train a full network, remove redundant neurons or connections, and fine-tune (Han et al., 2015; Li et al., 2017). This requires at least two full training cycles.

Neural Architecture Search (NAS) methods (Zoph and Le, 2017; Liu et al., 2019) automate topology selection but are computationally expensive, often requiring thousands of GPU-hours. Recent training-free NAS approaches (Mellor et al., 2021; Abdelfattah et al., 2021) use proxy scores to evaluate architectures without training, but focus on selecting from a predefined search space rather than progressively discovering minimal topologies.

I propose the Random Cloud method, which takes a different approach: generate many networks with random weights, evaluate which ones classify best without any training, progressively reduce their topology by removing neurons, and refine only the best minimal candidate with backpropagation at the end. The key insight is that among a large enough “cloud” of randomly initialized networks, some will exhibit non-trivial classification accuracy even without training—and these networks can be structurally reduced while maintaining that accuracy.

The contributions of this work are:

  • •

    A pre-training structural pruning method that discovers minimal topologies without training the full network.

  • •

    An empirical evaluation on 7 datasets showing the method matches or outperforms magnitude and random pruning baselines with lower computational cost.

  • •

    Statistical validation with 10 seeds per configuration and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests.

2 Method

2.1 Overview

Given an initial topology 𝐭0=[n0,n1,…,nL]\mathbf{t}_{0}=[n_{0},n_{1},\ldots,n_{L}] for a feedforward network with L−1L{-}1 hidden layers, the Random Cloud method proceeds in three phases:

Phase 1: Exploration. Generate NN networks {R1,…,RN}\{R_{1},\ldots,R_{N}\} with random weights drawn from 𝒰⁡(−1,1)\mathcal{U}(-1,1). For each network, evaluate its classification accuracy on the training set without any training (forward pass only). Then progressively reduce the topology by removing nelimn_{\text{elim}} neurons from the last hidden layer with available neurons, reconstruct the network (preserving the top-left submatrix of weights), and re-evaluate. Repeat until no further reduction is possible. Track the best-performing network that exceeds a threshold θ\theta.

Phase 2: Selection. Among all explored networks across the cloud, select the one with the highest accuracy that exceeds θ\theta, with the smallest topology.

Phase 3: Refinement. Train the selected network with standard backpropagation for EE epochs.

2.2 Algorithm

Topology reduction follows a sequential policy: remove nelimn_{\text{elim}} neurons from the last hidden layer with neurons >0>0. When that layer reaches 0, move to the previous hidden layer. Input and output layers are never modified.

Reconstruction preserves the existing structure: when reducing layer ll from nln_{l} to nl′n_{l}^{\prime} neurons, the weight matrix Wl∈ℝnl×nl−1W_{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{l}\times n_{l-1}} is truncated to Wl[1:nl′,:]W_{l}[1{:}n_{l}^{\prime},:] and the outgoing weights Wl+1[:,1:nl′]W_{l+1}[:,1{:}n_{l}^{\prime}] are similarly truncated. This preserves the top-left submatrix of the original weights.

Key difference from pruning: Magnitude pruning (Han et al., 2015) and random pruning operate post-training: they require training the full network, then pruning, then fine-tuning (two training cycles on the full topology). The Random Cloud operates pre-training: it evaluates with forward passes only (no backpropagation) and trains only the reduced network once.

3 Experiments

3.1 Setup

I evaluate on 7 classification datasets spanning binary (Breast Cancer, Sonar, Ionosphere, Adult Income) and multiclass (Iris, Wine, Optical Digits) problems, with dimensionality from 4 to 104 features and sizes from 150 to 45K samples. All datasets use 80/20 stratified train/test splits.

Methods compared: (1) Full Training: train the initial topology for EE epochs; (2) Magnitude Pruning: train full network, remove neurons with lowest L2 norm of incoming weights to match the Cloud’s target topology, fine-tune for EE epochs; (3) Random Pruning: same as magnitude but remove neurons randomly (average of 5 runs); (4) Random Cloud: the proposed method with cloud size N=50N{=}50.

All methods use the same total training budget (EE epochs) and the same target topology (discovered by the Cloud) for fair comparison. I report Accuracy, macro-averaged F1-score, and AUC-ROC. Each configuration is run with 10 different seeds; I report mean±\pmstd and Wilcoxon signed-rank pp-values.

3.2 Results

3.3 Statistical Significance

Table 2 reports results over 10 seeds with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests comparing the Cloud against each baseline.

The Cloud significantly outperforms both baselines on Sonar (p=0.017p{=}0.017 vs magnitude, p=0.005p{=}0.005 vs random), the dataset with the highest parameter reduction (87.2%). On Ionosphere, Wine, and Optical Digits, the differences are not statistically significant—all methods perform similarly at the target topology. On Adult Income, magnitude pruning has a slight edge in accuracy (p=0.028p{=}0.028) but not in F1-score (p=0.508p{=}0.508), suggesting the difference does not affect minority class performance.

3.4 Computational Cost

The Cloud is faster than full training in 4 of 5 datasets because it only trains the reduced network. Pruning baselines are always 1.5–1.8×\times slower because they require training the full network and fine-tuning the pruned one. The Cloud’s exploration phase (forward passes without backpropagation) accounts for only 25–44% of total time.

4 Analysis and Limitations

Why it works. With sigmoid activations, network outputs are bounded in (0,1)(0,1) regardless of weight magnitudes. This means randomly initialized networks produce valid probability-like outputs, and among a cloud of 50 networks, some will exhibit non-trivial classification accuracy by chance. The progressive reduction then identifies which neurons are truly necessary.

Hyperparameter robustness. The method is insensitive to the accuracy threshold θ\theta in the range [0.3,0.6][0.3,0.6] (identical results across this range on all datasets). Cloud size N≥25N\geq 25 is sufficient; the sweet spot is N=50−100N{=}50{-}100. Eliminating 1 neuron per step produces the best compression.

Limitations. In high-dimensional input spaces (784 features in MNIST), the training-free evaluation signal degrades: with 1K samples, the Cloud loses 17pp vs magnitude pruning. With 5K samples, the gap closes to 0.6pp. The method’s sweet spot is tabular data with moderate dimensionality (30–104 features), where training-free evaluation provides sufficient signal and the savings from not training the full network are significant.

5 Related Work

Post-training pruning. Magnitude pruning (Han et al., 2015) removes weights with small magnitudes after training. Structured pruning (Li et al., 2017) removes entire filters/neurons. Both require training the full network first. The proposed method avoids this cost entirely.

Lottery Ticket Hypothesis. Frankle and Carlin (2019) showed that sparse subnetworks (“winning tickets”) exist within randomly initialized networks that can be trained to full accuracy. Finding them requires iterative train-prune-reset cycles. The Random Cloud searches for viable topologies (not specific weight configurations) in a single pass.

Training-free NAS. Mellor et al. (2021) and Abdelfattah et al. (2021) propose zero-cost proxies to score architectures without training. These methods select from a predefined search space. The proposed method instead discovers the minimal topology through progressive reduction, which is complementary.

Random networks. The observation that random networks can exhibit structure is related to the theory of random features (Rahimi and Recht, 2007) and the edge of chaos in neural networks (Poole et al., 2016). This work exploits that observation empirically for architecture search.

6 Conclusion

This paper presented the Random Cloud method for finding minimal neural network topologies without training. The method generates a cloud of randomly initialized networks, evaluates them without backpropagation, progressively reduces their topology, and refines only the best candidate. On 7 classification benchmarks, it matches or outperforms magnitude and random pruning in 6 of 7 datasets, with statistically significant gains on Sonar (+4.9+4.9pp, p=0.017p{=}0.017) and lower computational cost (0.67–0.94×\times full training). The method is robust to hyperparameters and requires no tuning beyond default values.

The main limitation is scalability to high-dimensional inputs, where the training-free evaluation signal weakens. Future work includes exploring alternative reduction policies (magnitude-based neuron selection within the cloud), extending to convolutional architectures, and theoretical analysis of when training-free evaluation provides sufficient signal for topology search.

Reproducibility. The implementation in Julia (RandomCloud.jl) with all experiments, seeds, and baselines is available at https://github.com/Jastxz/random-cloudRandom Cloud repository.
